messages.content:
Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 27
  gender: Non-binary
  ethnicity: Oceania
  relationship_status: In a relationship
  occupation: Special Education Teacher
  trauma_type: Stalking
  pcl5: 34

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Being Followed: Feeling followed or tracked, Being Watched: Feeling watched or observed, Auditory (Footsteps): Footsteps behind or nearby
  Maladaptive Strategies: Rumination: Prevention: ruminate about how event could have been prevented, Avoid Relaxation: avoid relaxing because it feels dangerous, Checking Surroundings: constantly scan environment for signs of threat
  Threat: Scanning for Danger: I constantly scan my surroundings for signs of danger, Hypervigilance: Being superalert or watchful or on guard, Threat in Movements: Sudden movements by others put me immediately on guard
  Memory: Fragmented Pieces: My memories of the event come in disconnected pieces that do not fit together, Partial Clarity: Some moments of the event are extremely clear while others are completely blank, Incomplete Picture: I feel like I am only remembering parts of what happened and the rest is missing

Vignette:
Aroha Tane is a 27-year-old non-binary Māori-American special education teacher who presented for an initial psychological assessment following a period of sustained stalking by a former acquaintance that ended approximately eight months prior. They came to the first session quietly watchful, choosing a seat facing the door, and spoke in measured, careful sentences — as though each word required checking before release.

The stalking had unfolded over nearly four months. What began as unwanted messages escalated into the acquaintance appearing outside Aroha's apartment building, then outside their school, then in the parking lot where they walked to their car each evening after their students had been collected by their families. Aroha had never been certain how the person always knew where they were. That uncertainty became its own wound. There were evenings when Aroha would hear footsteps on the stairwell of their building and stand completely still inside their apartment, listening, trying to calculate whether the rhythm belonged to a neighbour or to him. Sometimes the footsteps would stop on their floor, and Aroha would not breathe. The police were involved twice; the situation eventually resolved through a restraining order and the acquaintance relocating, but by then the four months had left something restructured inside Aroha that legal paperwork could not reach.

What Aroha finds most disorienting now is that the memories of the stalking do not form a coherent story they can hold and examine. Certain moments arrive with terrible precision — the particular sound of footsteps slowing behind them on a quiet street, the sight of a familiar car idling near the school entrance — while whole weeks of that period are simply absent, as though their mind had been recording intermittently. Aroha described feeling like they were trying to assemble something from pieces that don't belong to the same puzzle. This incompleteness troubles them deeply; they find themselves turning the fragments over repeatedly, trying to reconstruct what they might have missed, what signs they failed to read, what different decision might have made the whole thing impossible. This mental rehearsal of prevention occupies long stretches of their evenings and commutes, though it yields nothing except exhaustion.

At school, where Aroha works closely with students who require attentive, regulated adult presence, the hypervigilance has become both professionally disruptive and personally isolating. The classroom has large windows that face the school's main car park, and Aroha now positions themselves throughout the day so that the windows remain in their peripheral vision. When a teaching assistant crosses the room quickly to redirect a student, Aroha's body responds before their mind can intervene — a sharp internal lurch, muscles tensing, attention fragmenting from whatever instruction they were giving. Colleagues have noticed that Aroha seems distracted. One gently asked whether everything was all right, and Aroha deflected, aware that explaining felt both impossible and dangerous, as though naming it would confirm that the threat was still present.

At home, Aroha's partner has noticed that they no longer settle. Evenings that once involved cooking together or watching something on the couch now find Aroha moving through the apartment in irregular circuits, checking the locks, listening. Aroha had come to believe that relaxing — truly relaxing, the kind that loosens attention — was something they could not afford. The feeling of being watched had not departed with the restraining order; it had simply become untethered from any specific person, free to attach itself to any stranger walking behind them on the footpath, any car that seemed to slow, any set of footsteps in a public space. Aroha knows, intellectually, that the threat has passed. But the body does not know this, and Aroha has stopped trusting the body's ignorance as safe.

What finally brought Aroha to seek help was a moment at school three weeks ago when a student — a child they adore, one who sometimes approaches from behind to take their hand — caused Aroha to spin around with a gasp that frightened the child. Aroha spent the rest of that afternoon in a state of quiet devastation. They came to the first session saying they were most afraid that something essential had been permanently altered in them. What they most hoped for, offered carefully at the end of the session, was to feel safe enough to stop watching.
